title: Intarsia stripe scarf
subtitle: A flat scarf with bold vertical colour blocks in intarsia.
excerpt: A scarf knitted flat in three-colour intarsia on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide by 150 cm long. Three vertical colour blocks of equal width run the full length of the scarf, each block worked from its own yarn bobbin. Intarsia produces a single-layer fabric with no floats across the colour changes.
sourceNotes: Vertical colour-block intarsia knitting is documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) under intarsia technique, citations only. Victorian comforter and scarf patterns did not commonly use vertical intarsia divisions; the modern intarsia stripe scarf is a 20th-century design form.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat colourwork technique in which separate yarn bobbins are used for each colour section. The yarns are not stranded across the row; instead, at each colour boundary the two yarns are twisted around each other to link the sections without leaving a gap.
The point on a row where one colour ends and the next begins. In intarsia, the two yarns must be twisted at the join to prevent a gap from opening.
A small spool, card, or butterfly wind of yarn used for one colour section in intarsia knitting. Using bobbins prevents the separate yarn lengths from tangling.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a scarf knitted flat in three-colour
intarsia
on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide and 150 cm long. Three vertical colour blocks of 12 stitches each run the full length, each worked from its own
bobbin
of yarn. At each
colour join
the two yarns are twisted once around each other on the wrong side to close the vertical seam between blocks.

Flat construction is essential for intarsia: the technique only works on flat rows where the yarn bobbins can hang at rest on the wrong side. In-the-round intarsia is possible but significantly more complex. The finished scarf needs about 180 m (approximately 110 g) each of three aran-weight colours.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight yarn, colour A
items.substitutions: Any aran-weight yarn. Smooth yarn gives the cleanest intarsia colour joins.

items.name: 5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 6 / US 8)
Yarn bobbins
items.substitutions: Small squares of card or butterfly winds work equally well.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 24 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. The intarsia fabric knits at the same gauge as plain stocking stitch because only one yarn is in use at a time across each section. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 1.1 cm at this stitch count. Row gauge is important: 24 rows per 10 cm across 360 body rows gives the 150 cm length.
Pattern
Cast on
Using a separate yarn length for each colour, use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 12 stitches in colour A, then 12 stitches in colour B, then 12 stitches in colour C. Alternatively, cast on all 36 stitches in one colour and join the other colours on the first row: work 12 stitches then drop the old colour, join the new colour with a twist at the boundary, and continue. The latter method is easier for most beginners.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Body
RS row: K12 A, twist B over A at the join (carry B over A from back), K12 B, twist C over B at the join, K12 C. (36 sts)
WS row: P12 C, twist B over C at the join, P12 B, twist A over B at the join, P12 A. (36 sts)

Note the twist direction reverses on RS and WS rows: on RS bring the new colour under the old from the left; on WS bring the new colour under the old from the right. Consistent twist direction in each row keeps the join neat.
Repeat RS and WS rows until the scarf measures 150 cm. At the halfway mark (approximately row 180 of 360 body rows), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 180 you should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a standard bind-off in stocking stitch across all 36 stitches, switching colours at the 12-stitch boundaries to match the colour blocks.
Common faults

Gap at the colour join. The two yarns must be twisted (one carried over or under the other) at every join on every row without exception. A single missed twist leaves a vertical gap that cannot be closed without re-knitting.

Yarn bobbins tangling at the wrong side. The three bobbins hang at the back and wrap around each other as you turn the work. Untwist the bobbins before beginning each row rather than correcting mid-row. Keep bobbins small — no more than 2 m at a time — to reduce the tangling mass.

Colour joins pulling tighter than the blocks. The twist at the join can gather the fabric if pulled too firmly. The yarn carried over the other should be looped loosely, not pulled taut. Work the first stitch after each join at normal tension.
Finishing

Weave in all tails from cast-on and bind-off along the wrong side within the matching colour block. Block lightly: pin the scarf flat to the finished dimensions and steam or wet block. The stocking stitch blocks will be fully flat after blocking.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. The intarsia joins are most vulnerable to stress when wet; do not wring.
What to try next
